beats.text: On the morning of June the fourth, 1942, four Japanese aircraft carriers were sailing toward a tiny island in the middle of the Pacific.

v.q: The Battle of Midway 1942 John Ford

beats.text: By that evening, all four were burning.
The films tell it as a miracle. A lucky dive at the perfect second, five minutes before Japan would have won.
The real story is stranger. It was won by a fake message about drinking water, a ship that should not have been there, and a pilot who followed a single wake across the sea.
Six months earlier, Japan had struck Pearl Harbor. Since then, it had not lost a single major battle.
Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto wanted to finish the job. He would take Midway and lure the surviving American carriers out to be destroyed.
Midway was a small atoll, two little islands and a lagoon, about thirteen hundred miles from Hawaii.
But it was the last American outpost before Pearl Harbor itself.
Yamamoto sent a huge force. Carriers, battleships, transports, and a strike at Alaska to pull eyes away.
